Broncos news: What Sean Payton said about getting bailed out by refs in Week 3 vs. Rams appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton knows all too well what it is like to be on the wrong end of a controversial call. However, during Sunday night's 33-30 comeback win over the Los Angeles Rams, the tables may have turned.

Denver trailed 26-23 when quarterback Bo Nix appeared to throw toward the sideline on a third-down play. Los Angeles defensive back Josh Wallace intercepted the pass and appeared to secure the ball with both feet inbounds. However, Wallace was flagged for defensive pass interference against Broncos wide receiver Pat Bryant, wiping out the apparent interception. Nix later scored the game-winning touchdown.

The sequence immediately drew comparisons to the 2018 NFC Championship Game between Payton's New Orleans Saints and the Rams. In that game, a late pass interference against Los Angeles went uncalled, helping the Rams advance to the Super Bowl. The parallels were hard to miss, as referee Bill Vinovich, who officiated the 2018 matchup, alsc worked Sunday's contest.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Payton was asked Monday whether the latest situation reminded him of the infamous no-call.

"Well this is years later, so a completely different game, different players. I think there were two calls really that I guess that a lot of people were looking at, one over on Pat Bryant's side and then the one that was a little bit later," said Payton.

Rather than dwell on officiating decisions, Payton said his approach is to focus on penalties Denver can control.

"Each week when these things come up… The longer you get in this thing, the less you discuss penalties. You just got to go out and play. I've yet to see one get changed either way. You hope that when the game's over with, the season's over with, you're on the positive side of the ledger. I focus a little bit more on the penalties that we can control relative to pre-snap, post-snap, those types of things, but that's really where I sit with it."

The Broncos eventually overcame a 16-0 halftime deficit, scoring 30 points over the final two quarters to complete the stunning comeback.

title: Lions Cut Ties With DB Who Appeared in 17 Games Last Season
description: The Detroit Lions parted ways with defensive back Natrone Brooks one day after they defeated the New York Jets. The post Lions Cut Ties With DB Who Appeared in 17 Games Last Season appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Detroit Lions are making some roster moves after a win over the New York Jets.

The Lions announced on Monday that they parted ways with a practice squad defensive back, making room for a new addition to the tight end room.

The Lions have been hit hard by injuries to their secondary, but cut into their depth a bit after Sunday's win.

"Lions have released DB Natrone Brooks from the Practice Squad and signed TE Miles Kitselman to the Practice Squad," the team announced in a post on X.

The Lions parted ways with cornerback Natrone Brooks, a 26-year-old who spent the first two seasons of his career with the Atlanta Falcons. Brooks appeared in 17 games last season with one start, making 10 total tackles.

The Lions made a series of other roster moves before Brooks was released. The team placed defensive back Avonte Maddox on injured reserve after he suffered an injury in the Week 2 loss to the Buffalo Bills, blowing another hole in a secondary that was already missing starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph.

The team also placed Thomas Harper on injured reserve, then elevated safety Jalen Mills from the practice squad for Sunday's game.

The 32-year-old Mills had just joined the practice squad earlier in the week, but reporter Josh Helmer of USA Today's Lions Wire noted that he has plenty of experience under his belt.

"Originally a seventh-round pick out of LSU by the Eagles in 2016, Mills has played in 122 games and started 92, registering 460 tackles, 60 passes defended, 10 tackles for loss, eight interceptions, seven quarterback hits, three forced fumbles, 1.5 sacks, and one fumble recovery," Helmer wrote. "He has also returned one interception for a touchdown."

The Lions used the open spot on the practice squad to add Kitselman, an undrafted rookie tight end out of Tennessee. NFL.com draft expert Lance Zierlein predicted that Kitselman could grow into a solid backup or special teams regular.

"Kitselman has good size and will play as a connected tight end on the next level," Zierlein wrote. "He needs to play with better hand placement and pad level, but he's willing to put in work in-line or as a move blocker. He has above-average play speed in space and showed an ability to run a variety of routes. He has enough speed to stress man coverage into the second level. His separation underneath is average, though. Drops, double-catches and issues securing contested throws were evident in 2025. Kitselman has Day 3 draft value and could find work as a TE3/4."

title: Cardinals' late offensive launch led to another loss at Levi’s Stadium
description: The Arizona Cardinals have offensive woes that are leading to worry but head coach Mike LaFleur can avoid things from worsening.
fullText:
Arizona Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur is working through the kinks to get his hands around the offensive scheme in his first season. Yet, another slow offensive start versus a divisional foe in the San Francisco 49ers caused a scoring deficit that ultimately became insurmountable in the 36-30 loss.

Six total points in the first half was not nearly enough to keep the 49ers at bay on their home field at Levi's Stadium. The Cardinals defense has struggled somewhat and it's not primarily because they are lacking in talent, but that they're spending long durations of time on the field and because their offensive colleagues have been unable to cannot sustain drives. The Cardinals defense also has not played many game minutes with a scoring league, leaving them susceptible to the opponents will in both run game and pass.

Injuries-riddled last year on defense and with the pending surgery of second-year defensive back Will Johnson, it seems that the Cardinals' trajectory will be duplicated in 2026. Thus, LaFleur badly needs his offense to pick up the pace to compensate. As of now, the Cardinals rank No. 24 in yards per game and sit at No. 19 in points per game.

The Cardinals are now 1-3, but thankfully the Seattle Seahawks slipped up against the Washington Commanders, giving them some slight grace in the divisional race. However, the 49ers have now advanced to 3-0, and it'll be hard for any of the NFC West division teams to catch them if they continue at this pace. Speaking of pace, LaFleur needs to better prepare offensively for pending opponents so that his battered defensive unit doesn't participate in every contest playing from a deficit.

title: Senate passes the Protect College Sports Act
description: Report says there's a "0.0 percent chance" the House passes it before election day in November.
fullText:
Big-time college sports has moved halfway toward the federal bailout they crave. The rest of the journey is unlikely to happen soon.

The U.S. Senate passed the so-called "Protect College Sports Act" on Monday night, by a vote of 77-22. The bill now goes to the U.S. House of Representatives.

Earlier in the day, Pat Forde of SI.com cited an unnamed source who said that there is a "0.0 percent chance" the House will pass the bill before the midterm elections.

With the Democrats widely expected to seize control of the House in November, the question then becomes whether it will do any meaningful business before the next Congress convenes in January.

So there's still a long way to go before the NCAA and its members get the antitrust exemption and other benefits designed to stave off a catastrophe. Even as college football is more popular and profitable than ever.

There's chaos, they say. From whose perspective? The players, after years of being exploited by a system that denied them the opportunity to participate meaningfully in the value they generate, are sitting pretty. It's not chaotic for them; it's the free market in operation.

But the schools apparently can't be trusted to balance their budgets, which is bullshit. Every American business faces an ongoing challenge to adapt or fail. In lieu of expecting the administrators to come up with a better way to carve up the pie and/or to spend within their means, they want artificial restrictions on what the players can make.

That's not how it should be. And, despite the Senate vote, maybe it won't be.

Few players are under as much pressure as Kawhi Leonard entering this NBA season. A fresh start with the Toronto Raptors sees Leonard trying to put his controversial past behind him. Media members wanting to ask about Kawhi's punishment for breaking salary cap rules with the Los Angeles Clippers got shut down right away.

Leonard opened his Raptors media day press conference with the following message:

"Hey, everyone. Thanks for coming. I know I'm excited to be here. I know why some of you guys came. You want to hear about the investigation, but talking with the NBA and the PA, I think the best decision is to move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor.

I already was a distraction for the past 70 days and wasn't able to meet my teammates, do any of that mini-camp stuff with them. So moving forward, I just want to talk about the Toronto Raptors today. They released a statement that you can go back to and look at. Like I said, I just want to focus on basketball again and being a Toronto Raptor."

Kawhi wanted to only discuss things pertaining to the Raptors' upcoming season. Despite the Clippers' punishment being a massive story, Leonard got away without having to discuss it. Kawhi instead focused on praising teammates Scottie Barnes and RJ Barrett.

The most interesting aspect of Leonard's quote is that he acknowledged talking with the league and the player's association. All parties agreed he wouldn't discuss the Clippers after he was officially traded for Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick.

Kawhi seemingly got away with breaking the rules with a light punishment of a fine. The Clippers losing five draft picks will see Leonard never having to address that now. Steve Ballmer and the Clippers franchise are left answering all questions with minimal hope.

Things have progressed for Kawhi to pretend this didn't happen and put it fully behind him. The Raptors traded for Leonard to bring back the 2019 NBA Finals MVP. Toronto is the only market expected to cheer Kawhi to make it logical why he wanted to return.

The next question for this saga will play out when the Raptors visit the Clippers in the season. Leonard is up there with Chris Paul and Bob McAdoo among the greatest players in franchise history.

However, the way that Kawhi left the Clippers in basketball hell has turned him into a villain for the fan base. Leonard refusing to speak about them now will only make that hostile feeling even worse.

Clippers fans will most likely boo Kawhi loudly and heckle him with chants when he's back. The way that Leonard handled this situation also is going to block a future jersey retirement. Clippers fans are entering this season hoping that rookie Keaton Wagler can save the season after Kawhi set the franchise on fire. Leonard is hoping to distance himself from this and become relevant for title contention this season.

fullText:
Panthers' inexcusable loss to Browns delivers harsh truth about Bryce Young appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

The Carolina Panthers did almost everything necessary to beat the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. Sadly, they did not finish the job. That is precisely why their 21-18 loss at Huntington Bank Field feels so damaging. Carolina outgained Cleveland 360-259 and rallied from a 10-0 deficit to take an 18-13 lead with less than five minutes remaining. They appeared to have the Browns beaten when Akayleb Evans intercepted Deshaun Watson in the end zone. Then everything unraveled. A roughing-the-passer penalty erased the turnover. Watson engineered the winning drive. Bryce Young threw the interception that ended Carolina's final opportunity with nine seconds left. For Young, this was a sobering reminder that impressive statistics do not automatically translate into winning quarterback play. He did plenty to keep Carolina competitive. He did not do enough to finish the game.

Young's final numbers were not too shabby. He had 26 completions on 48 attempts for 290 yards, one touchdown, and two interceptions. However, the context makes them considerably less impressive. Carolina repeatedly moved the football without consistently turning those possessions into touchdowns. This forced Ryan Fitzgerald to convert four field goals to keep the Panthers within striking distance. The Panthers also went just 4-for-15 on third down and failed on both of their fourth-down attempts.

That is the central issue confronting Young. The Browns recorded three sacks, six tackles for loss, and five passes defensed on him. Mason Graham produced two sacks and repeatedly collapsed the interior pocket. Young had opportunities to make the defense pay. Carolina, though, too often settled for field goals instead of touchdowns.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

The circumstances were admittedly difficult. Xavier Legette was inactive, while Jalen Coker left with a quad injury. Carolina's receiving options became increasingly limited as the game progressed. Yet that is precisely when Young is expected to elevate the players around him. He moved the ball between the twenties, but the Panthers repeatedly stalled once Cleveland tightened the windows.

To Young's credit, he delivered the kind of response Carolina desperately needed in the fourth quarter. With the Panthers trailing 13-12, he orchestrated a six-play, 72-yard drive that culminated in an eight-yard touchdown pass to John Metchie III with 4:25 remaining. Suddenly, Carolina had an 18-13 advantage and seemingly had control of the game.

Then came the moment that changed everything. After Cleveland drove inside the red zone, it appeared Carolina had finally slammed the door when Evans intercepted Watson in the end zone. Instead, linebacker Bobby Okereke was flagged for roughing the passer, wiping away the turnover. Three plays later, Watson found Harold Fannin Jr for the 14-yard go-ahead touchdown.

Young still received one final opportunity. Carolina got the ball back and needed only a field goal to force overtime. Instead, Cleveland's pressure closed in. Young's final pass was tipped by Derek Barnett before Ronnie Hickman secured the game-clinching interception. That final sequence demonstrated just how difficult it remained for Young to consistently create when the pocket became compressed. The truth is Young still has to prove he can consistently close games when conditions are far from ideal.

This is not an argument that Young is incapable of becoming the quarterback Carolina envisioned. His performance through the first three weeks provides plenty of evidence that he can operate this offense efficiently and produce significant yardage. He also showed genuine poise by leading the late touchdown drive that temporarily put Carolina ahead.

Sunday, though, exposed the next hurdle in his development. Great quarterbacks eventually have to turn production into control. They have to recognize when the defense is dictating terms, protect the football when a field goal is enough, convert critical third downs and make the decisive throw when the game is hanging in the balance. Young did not consistently do that against Cleveland.

The Panthers also cannot place all of this defeat on their quarterback. The roughing-the-passer penalty was devastating. The fourth-down decisions were questionable. Injuries compromised the offense. Carolina's defense ultimately allowed Watson to engineer the decisive drive. This was a team loss.

Still, a quarterback like Young occupies a different place in the equation. Carolina is now 1-2, with the Detroit Lions coming to town next Sunday night. The Panthers just need Young to become more efficient when the field shrinks and more decisive when pressure arrives.

Until that happens, the uncomfortable reality is that Bryce Young can produce impressive numbers. That said, the Panthers still have not seen enough evidence that he can consistently turn those numbers into victories when the game is on the line.

The Philadelphia Eagles were trying to stay within one score of Chicago when a hard hit forced their starting quarterback off the field. Jalen Hurts had been moving the offense before taking contact near the sideline during the second quarter.

Hurts was sent for a concussion evaluation, forcing Andy Dalton to enter with Philadelphia in scoring position. The Eagles suddenly had to finish an important red-zone drive without their starting quarterback.

Hurts took the hit from Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson while scrambling toward the sideline. Jackson made contact as Hurts went out of bounds, and the quarterback was immediately sent for an evaluation.

#Eagles QB Jalen Hurts got leveled by D’Marco Jackson on a late hit and is now being evaluated for a concussion.

Andy Dalton is in.pic.twitter.com/s55XNVqqIc

— Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) September 29, 2026

Hurts returned to his feet and initially tried to rejoin the huddle. However, he had to go through the NFL's concussion evaluation process before he could continue playing.

Jackson was penalized for the hit, but the call was offset by a holding penalty against Philadelphia. Dalton then entered the game with the Eagles already deep in Chicago territory.

Philadelphia reached the 1-yard line, but Dalton's pass into the end zone was intercepted by Bears rookie safety Dillon Thieneman. It was Thieneman's first NFL interception and kept Chicago ahead 7-0.

The turnover showed why Hurts' absence mattered immediately. Philadelphia had moved into position to score, but Dalton had to finish the drive with little time to prepare.

Hurts was later cleared to return. Before leaving the game, he had completed 5 of 7 passes for 46 yards without a touchdown or interception.

Hurts returned before halftime and quickly helped Philadelphia cut into Chicago's lead. With one second remaining in the half, he scored on a quarterback sneak to make the score 10-7.

The sequence changed quickly for the Eagles. Hurts went from taking a hard hit and leaving for an evaluation to watching Dalton throw a red-zone interception before returning to score a touchdown.

The important distinction is that Hurts was evaluated for a concussion, not diagnosed with one. He completed the league's evaluation process and received clearance to return.

Philadelphia avoided a longer absence for its starting quarterback. However, the play showed how quickly the game could have changed if Hurts had not been cleared.

Dalton was forced into an important red-zone situation with little warning, and his interception allowed Chicago to protect its lead. Hurts' return ended the Eagles' immediate quarterback concern, but Jackson's hit gave Philadelphia a serious scare before halftime.

title: Jim Harbaugh still trusts Mike McDaniel, wants Justin Herbert to 'be better'
description: Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh says he isn't planning to take any control away from offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel despite the team's struggles.
fullText:
It's never good when NFL coaches on struggling teams have to publicly reaffirm their faith in members of their staff before the calendar turns to October — and that's what Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh did on Monday.

Speaking to reporters in the wake of a 24-16 loss to the Buffalo Bills, Harbaugh was asked if he would consider taking some control away from offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel if the offense doesn't improve.

"No, we trust Mike. We believe in Mike," Harbaugh said.

It would be odd for Harbaugh to publicly admit to anything else at this point, especially because he's not in a good position to do much else to salvage the season. Harbaugh has never called plays at the NFL level and must hope McDaniel and Justin Herbert can fix the NFL's No. 21-ranked offense (309 yards per game) if the Chargers have any chance of becoming the eighth team in NFL history to reach the postseason after an 0-3 start.

"We're searching for every possible way to give ourselves an advantage," Harbaugh said. "Every possible way to not beat ourselves."

Although Harbaugh doesn't see himself intervening on McDaniel's turf, he does want to see improvement from Herbert. The quarterback struggled against the Bills, failing to capitalize on five takeaways from the Chargers' defense. He passed for 226 yards with a touchdown and an interception, but four trips to the red zone — two of which were assisted by favorable field position off takeaways — resulted in only three field goals and a touchdown.

"To be better," said Harbaugh, regarding Herbert's decision-making. "That drives Justin, that drives me, that drives his position coach, that drives Mike [McDaniel]. ... I mean, drives us all."

Herbert isn't the only underperformer. Dropped passes from wide receiver Quentin Johnston and tight end Oronde Gadsden II were factors in the Bills becoming the first team since the Jacksonville Jaguars in the 2022 season wild-card playoffs to win despite five turnovers and a minus-four turnover differential.

The team the Jaguars beat that January? The Chargers.

The potential was there from the beginning, as evidenced by their No. 10 draft selection in the 2025 NBA Draft. They knew the expectation. They knew the potential and ambition to be that star center in the league.

But slowly but surely, Maluach got his time in the G League, and even stints during the back end of the season proved that the gamble could pay off.

Even getting in the playoffs, he made a lasting impression. So once Summer League came around, a breakout was expected, and boy did Phoenix get one.

In Las Vegas, Maluach and the Suns' young group caught the league in a frenzy. The dominance was on display.

Although the talent was coming to fruition, it's the process that everyone is starstruck by. He knows what will work, how to navigate his screens, and how to position himself in a pick-and-roll scenario.

Maluach still asks the questions, even when knowing the answers. His rise immediately caught the attention of fellow teammates like Luke Kennard and Pat Spencer, who all echoed a familiar statement during media: he is the guy on the breakout watch.

Talent can take a player only so far. But what impresses most is this jovial, childlike energy that Maluach brings to the gym. Behind that energy is the confidence and swagger, mixed with striving to be better; it's cliché, but it's that way for a reason.

And striving to be better comes with taking advice from the franchise's best player, and one of the league's top guards is certainly worth paying attention to.

Not to mention, with just about every player talking about the physical, mental, and on-court leap they've seen, much of it comes back to his time with Booker.

"He's done this for a long time, and he has a lot of tools that I can learn from him as a center," Maluach explained during media day. "Just being able to go to him and just ask what I should do in this situation because he's that type of player in the NBA that will see different coverages every day.

"He's kind of like a coach himself, and I get to learn a lot from him. A lot of stuff that the coaches don't see that he sees as a player when he gets blitzed. Just being able to reach out to him and learn that and have more knowledge."

Second-year guys get hyped up, but not like this. Safe to say that it's full steam ahead for Maluach and his much-needed ascension, given the center depth taking a hit.

title: SEC, power conferences release statements after Protect College Sports Act passes Senate vote
description: After the Protect College Sports Act passed a full Senate vote 77-23 on Monday, each of the power conference released a statement praising the advancement. fullText:
After the Protect College Sports Act passed a full Senate vote 77-23 on Monday, each of the power conference released a statement praising the advancement. The bipartisan legislation will now head to the U.S. House of Representatives.

The power conferences all voiced their support for the Protect College Sports Act as it went through the Senate. At first, only the Big 12 and ACC were on board, but the SEC and Big Ten announced their full support in late July to give the bill some momentum. The NCAA also supported it and released its statement shortly after passage.

From there, the bill advanced out of a markup and committee vote, as well as multiple procedural votes. After debate and votes on amendments Monday, the legislation passed the Senate. It will now head to the House, which is not due back in session until after the midterm elections.

"The bipartisan Senate passage of the Protect College Sports Act represents an important step toward establishing a clear and durable national framework for college athletics," the SEC said in its statement. "We look forward to working with members of the House of Representatives to advance legislation that protects student-athletes, provides consistent national standards for universities and conferences, supports women's and Olympic sports, and strengthens the long-term future of college athletics.

"The SEC and our 16 member universities will remain actively and constructively engaged as the legislative process continues, with the goal of achieving a national framework that provides stability, accountability, and clarity for college sports."

In its statement, the Big Ten credited the Senators who sponsored the bill. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) introduced it in late May, and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.) and Chris Coons (D-Del.) joined as co-sponsors.

"We are pleased the Protect College Sports Act has passed the Senate, and are appreciative of the substantial work that has gone into the effort from the act's authors, sponsors, and supporters," the Big Ten's statement read. "We look forward to the next steps to passage as we continue to support the act as passed by the Senate."

Additionally, the Big 12 cited the importance of the Protect College Sports Act's advancement. The conference cited the need to "move beyond uncertainty" as the landscape continues to shift in the NIL and revenue-share eras.

"We are encouraged by the continued progress of the Protect College Sports Act and appreciate the bipartisan leadership of Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Cantwell, and others that has moved this effort forward," the Big 12's statement read. "The legislation provides a more stable national framework for college athletics, incorporates important transparency measures, and moves our industry closer to a sustainable model that supports student-athletes, institutions, conferences, and fans.

"The future of college sports depends on our ability to move beyond uncertainty and toward lasting solutions, and the Protect College Sports Act is an important step in that direction. We look forward to working with lawmakers as the process advances."

The Protect College Sports Act would grant the NCAA an antitrust exemption to limit athletes to one transfer without penalty, standardize the new five-year, age-based eligibility policy, increase the revenue-sharing cap to nearly $50, put more enforcement in place around the rev-share cap, create an agent registry with a maximum 5% fee and allow schools to pool together their media rights, among other things.

Three amendments were added to the Protect College Sports Act on Monday after the Senate voted on seven of them. One would increase the conference limit to 20 members, rather than the 19 members in the bill's initial text, and another would require schools to disclose foreign funding in college sports. The third would allow states to pass more health and safety requirements through statute and common law.

Up next for the Protect College Sports Act is the House of Representatives. However, the House moved to take two weeks out of its calendar and is not due back until November, after the midterm elections. Cruz has expressed optimism the House will return to vote on the legislation.

Should the bill advance out of the House, it would then head to President Donald Trump's desk. Trump has been a strong supporter of the legislation, and Cruz has suggested he sign it into law on ESPN's College GameDay.

title: Codie Taylor to lead New Zealand All Blacks in rugby's Bledisloe Cup despite Scott Barrett's return

fullText:
WELLINGTON, New Zealand (AP) — Hooker Codie Taylor will lead New Zealand in its two-test Bledisloe Cup series against Australia next month, and former captain Scott Barrett has been recalled after playing barely an hour of rugby all year.

Taylor was selected captain of the 34-strong All Blacks squad announced Tuesday for tests against the Wallabies in Auckland on Oct. 10 and Sydney on Oct. 17 in place of Ardie Savea, who is out of action after shoulder surgery.

Scott Barrett will rejoin his brothers Beauden and Jordie in an All Blacks squad for the first time this season after recovering from back surgery. He made his first appearance in 2026 last weekend for Taranaki province in the National Provincial Championship, playing just over 50 minutes.

Shannon Frizell has been recalled for the first time since 2023 to bolster a depleted backrow.

Apart from Savea, backrower Luke Jacobson and winger Caleb Clarke are sidelined for the remainder of the season. Flyhalf Ruben Love (ankle), lock Patrick Tuipulotu (calf), centers Anton Lienert-Brown (knee) and Billy Proctor (shoulder) and prop Ollie Norris (knee) also are unavailable for the Bledisloe Cup.

In Love's absence Beauden Barrett, Richie Mo'unga Damian McKenzie and the uncapped Josh Jacomb will vie for the No. 10 jersey, though McKenzie may be preferred at fullback.

The All Blacks are coming off the punishing four-test Greatest Rivalry series against South Africa, won 3-1 by the Springboks, and will face a Wallabies team heartened by their dramatic, upset win over South Africa last weekend.

Taylor led the All Blacks in Savea's absence in the final test of the series against South Africa, a 43-28 loss in Baltimore.

"Rugby's Greatest Rivalry tour was great for us," head coach Dave Rennie said. "We've learnt a lot about our game and about ourselves and it gave a lot of guys valuable time in the jersey. Plenty of them put their hands up, and every player selected fully deserves their place.

"It's great to welcome back Scott Barrett and Shannon Frizell. Scott has had a challenging stretch on the sidelines, and we're thrilled to have his experience and leadership back in the group. Shannon brings plenty of test experience and physical impact to our loose forwards.​"

Rennie described Taylor as "a top man who has huge mana (status). "

"His leadership was important for us during Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, so we know he will do an outstanding job in Ardie's absence."

New Zealand will be defending a 53-test winning streak at Auckland's Eden Park, dating back to 1994.

"The Bledisloe Cup means a huge amount to this team. We've held it since 2003 and we don't take that for granted," Rennie said.

"Australia will be a real challenge. It's now a very experienced Wallabies side who have played a lot of test footy together. After eight games on the road, we're excited to start this series in front of our home crowd at Eden Park."

title: How the Protect College Sports Act could affect Charlie Woods and college golf
description: A new Senate bill seeks to stabilize college sports amid NIL chaos, potentially impacting stars like Charlie Woods.
fullText:
TaylorMade's decision to sign Charlie Woods to an NIL deal looked significant when it was announced earlier this month. Now, with federal lawmakers moving closer to reshaping the entire college sports landscape, the agreement may look even more consequential.

The Protect College Sports Act cleared a major hurdle this week after passing the Senate and advancing to the House of Representatives, bringing college athletics a step closer to the most sweeping federal overhaul in years. Supporters say the legislation would bring stability to a system upended by unrestricted player movement, conference realignment and a rapidly evolving name, image and likeness marketplace.

In a 77-22 vote on Capitol Hill on Monday, Sept. 28, the years-long legislative proposal formally cleared its first major hurdle, with eight co-sponsors, headlined by the early work of Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.).

"The most important part of the bill is bringing order to chaos," Cruz told USA TODAY Sports. "College sports is the Wild West. There are essentially no rules. Litigation has struck down virtually all the rules, and as a result, you have athletes going into the transfer portal two, three, four times. You have athletes competing for seven or eight years. You have 27, 28-year-olds competing against 17-year-olds. You have pro players coming back and playing college sports, and every school is in a spending spiral where virtually every athletic department is losing millions of dollars. Many of them are losing tens of millions of dollars. It's unsustainable, and as a consequence, every week we see a different problem.

"Programs being canceled, we see women's sports being canceled. We see Olympic sports being canceled, and if Congress doesn't act within a few years, we will see hundreds of thousands of roster slots and scholarship positions going away, and that would be a tragedy. It would be a tragedy because every year right now we have roughly 500,000 college athletes in America."

For golf, the bill could have far-reaching implications.

When TaylorMade signed Woods, the son of 15-time major champion Tiger Woods, the move underscored how NIL opportunities have expanded beyond traditional revenue sports. Woods, who is committed to Florida State and entering his senior year of high school, became one of the most visible examples of a golfer leveraging his personal brand before arriving on a college campus.

At the time, the agreement signaled more than an equipment partnership. It reflected the growing value of elite amateur golfers as marketing assets. While top junior players have long received free clubs, balls and apparel from manufacturers, paid NIL agreements remain relatively rare in college golf. One Division I men's coach recently estimated that only a few dozen players currently have manufacturer deals that include compensation.

The Protect College Sports Act would not eliminate NIL opportunities such as Woods' partnership with TaylorMade. Athletes would still be free to pursue outside endorsement agreements and marketing relationships. Instead, the legislation seeks to establish a national framework for college athletics while providing additional revenue-sharing opportunities through schools, a move supporters believe would reduce uncertainty for athletes and athletic departments alike.

The bill also includes provisions aimed at protecting Olympic and non-revenue sports, a category that includes golf. Backers argue that without federal intervention, schools facing mounting financial pressure could be forced to reduce scholarships, cut roster spots or eliminate sports. The legislation would allow schools to direct additional revenue-sharing funds toward women's and Olympic sports, a measure supporters say could help preserve opportunities for future golfers.

That matters for players like Woods and the next generation of elite juniors. As NIL has transformed recruiting and athlete compensation, concerns have grown about whether smaller sports could lose ground while schools direct resources toward football and men's basketball. Supporters of the legislation contend that a more structured system could help maintain funding and scholarship opportunities across all sports.

The proposal still faces a vote in the House before it can reach President Donald Trump's desk, but its progress is another sign that the NIL era is entering a new phase.

title: Arizona State hockey players call for school to place coaches on administrative leave
description: In a letter to the school president, seven Arizona State hockey players disputed the school's review of Matthew Mayich's collapse during an August workout.
fullText:
Seven Arizona State hockey players have disputed aspects of the school's review of teammate Matthew Mayich's collapse during an offseason workout and have asked the university president to place the Sun Devils' coaching staff on administrative leave pending further investigation into the incident.

In a 26-page letter sent to Arizona State president Michael Crow on Monday, Sept. 28, the players said Mayich didn't receive water and received inadequate care after collapsing during an Aug. 20 workout due to heatstroke. Mayich remains on life support, with no chance of recovery.

The seven players, who account for about one-quarter of the Sun Devils' roster, filed the letter anonymously through Phoenix attorney Timothy Casey, out of fear of retaliation. All players have signed legal attestations stating that they were present at the workout.

MORE: Lawyer says ASU's narrative on Matthew Mayich's collapse is 'false'

In the letter, the players contested much of the university's preliminary account from senior vice president James Rund, which was publicly released on Sept. 22 and leveled no blame for what happened during the workout, which was led by an ex-Green Beret. The players said that Mayich was showing signs of distress and that coaches and staff who were present for the workout failed to follow the university's exertional heat illness policies before, during and after Mayich's collapse. After the workout, they said Arizona State coach Greg Powers minimized Mayich's condition and told them their teammate would be fine.

"This was not a team building session," Casey said to The Arizona Republic, which is part of the USA TODAY Network, on Sept. 28. "This was to break men down. It was full of sarcasm and ridicule. This was a perfect storm of cruelty and incompetency."

Emergency guidelines for treating heat illness call for immediate immersion in ice water, but the university found Mayich, who had no pre-existing medical conditions, was left lying on the ground as staff draped him in wet towels.

The Republic found that Tim Ziesel, the former Green Beret leading the workout, did not go through the required vetting process or sign standard forms. Instead, Ziesel's attorney said he was tasked with the workout based on a handshake agreement with Powers and other staff members.

Arizona State officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Republic about the letter.

The 21-year-old Mayich was a sophomore who was in his first season with the Sun Devils after transferring in from Clarkson University in Potsdam, New York.

In their letter, the players wrote that additional teammates share their concerns, but have similar fears about retaliation.

"We should not have to choose between telling the truth about August 20 and keeping what we have worked our whole lives for," the players wrote.

title: Pirates Are Looking Brilliant After Major Trade
description: Pittsburgh has often been sellers at the trade deadline due to a lack of relevance once July arrives. In these kinds of situations, the goal is always to dump off talent that may not be part of the future. In return, teams prefer to acquire young talent with loads of potential. Cherington did something in 2025 that is already looking like a home run. The post Pirates Are Looking Brilliant After Major Trade appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
The Pittsburgh Pirates finished the 2026 season with a record of 82-80. The end result did not end up being what the organization ultimately desired, however. The goal was always to get into the postseason and make a deep run in October. It was the first-ever year above .500 in the Ben Cherington era. He took over the front office in 2019, but he has not delivered what fans envisioned when the Pirates hired him. That doesn't mean, however, that he hasn't had some significant wins during his tenure.

Pittsburgh has often been sellers at the trade deadline due to a lack of relevance once July arrives. In these kinds of situations, the goal is always to dump off talent that may not be part of the future. In return, teams prefer to acquire young talent with loads of potential. Cherington did something in 2025 that is already looking like a home run based on recent events.

Ke'Bryan Hayes was a first-round selection of the Pirates back in 2015. He arrived in the big leagues in 2020, flashing a significant glove at third base. Unfortunately, he was very up and down on the offensive side. In April of 2022, he had done enough to earn a sizable eight-year, $70 million contract from the Pirates.

It really wasn't working out for Hayes in Pittsburgh as time went on. This led to him getting dealt to the Cincinnati Reds in 2025. The main piece of the deal coming back to the Steel City was middle infielder Sammy Stafura.

Fast forward to September of 2026, and Hayes is being called out for quite literally having one of the worst offensive seasons in baseball history. Bryce Spalding brought this up with a post on X.

"There has been 21,533 players since 1940 who have recorded 240 PA in a single season," Spalding wrote. "Ke'Bryan Hayes ranks 21,531/21,533 in wRC+ with his 13 wRC+ mark in 2026. His .419 OPS ranks 21,530/21,533. Quite literally a bottom 3 offensive season, EVER."

The wRC+ stat is an advanced hitting metric that essentially summarizes offensive production. Additionally, the Pirates later included Stafura in the deal to acquire Luke Weaver near the trade deadline. The reliever is under contract for 2027, so it seems to have worked out for the Pirates.

It hasn't been all sunshine and rainbows for the Pirates since Cherington took over. However, this is one of those moves that deserves to be lauded. Pittsburgh was able to shed Hayes' salary while also giving away someone who has no clue what he is doing at the plate.

The Buccos did not necessarily get a long-term prospect in the deal who is still around, but they were able to ditch Hayes. In addition, Weaver could very well be the closer for the franchise in 2027 — if baseball ends up being played.

Cherington catches a lot of heat, and he warrants most of it. The Pirates hired him to make a difference and bring winning baseball back to Pittsburgh. He hasn't accomplished that just yet; however, one of his best moves in recent memory made Hayes the Reds' problem.

title: Gordon Johncock, a two-time winner of the Indianapolis 500, has died at 90
description: Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 champion and winner of 25 career IndyCar races, has died.  Johncock died from natural causes Monday at his home in South Branch, Michigan, a spokesman for the family told The Associated Press.  Johncock competed in one of IndyCar's golden eras.
fullText:
INDIANAPOLIS (AP) — Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 champion and winner of 25 career IndyCar races, has died. He was 90.

Johncock died from natural causes Monday at his home in South Branch, Michigan, a spokesman for the family told The Associated Press.

Johncock competed in one of IndyCar's golden eras. He raced annually at The Brickyard against the likes of four-time winners A.J. Foyt, Rick Mears and Al Unser, three-time winners Bobby Unser and Johnny Rutherford and 1969 race winner Mario Andretti, among others.

And yet, with so many big personalities in the series then, Johncock managed to carve out his own niche with his smalltown roots and penchant for wearing flannel shirts and jeans. He won the 1976 USAC title in an IndyCar.

But he was best known for his Indy 500 wins. His first came in 1973, one of the race's most tragic months. His second came in 1982 when he outdueled Mears to the finish line for what was then the closest winning margin in race history at 0.16 seconds. It's still the seventh-closest.

"By far the biggest thrill of my racing career was winning Indianapolis in 1982," Johncock once said. "The way it happened, the competition, so many near wins after 1973 and it all came together and the car lasted in 1982. Plus, I've got amazing respect for Rick Mears — one of the very best. He was never my teammate, but I think we could have been good ones."

The month of May in 1973 was marred by rain, which forced the race to be run over three days and shortened to 133 of 200 laps; two horrific crashes that resulted in the deaths of drivers Art Pollard and Swede Savage, Johncock's teammate with Patrick Racing who was severely injured in the race. Savage was pronounced dead in early July.

A pit crew member for Patrick Racing also died after being hit by a fire truck responding to Savage's crash, And driver David "Salt" Walther suffered severe burns when his car burst into flames as it hit the catch fence in the front straightaway as the race began, injuring nearly a dozen fans.

Yet Johncock, who started 11th, overcame the chaos and was one of just two cars on the lead lap when more rain forced the race to be stopped.

"I didn't feel that race was given to us," Johncock once told Autoweek. "If we had only led one or two laps and happened to be settin' there when they stopped it and won it that way, then I guess you wouldn't have earned it very well."

Johncock started driving the family's John Deere tractor in Hastings, Michigan, when he was 5 years old. He joined the IndyCar Series in 1964 and finished fifth in the 500 as a rookie in 1965. Johncock wound up competing in the 500 24 times, tied for fifth-most. He made three starts on the front row, nine times on the second row and completed 7,895 miles while leading a total of 339 laps. He finished third in the 500 in 1976 and 1978, and had two fourth place finishes.

From 1964-92, Johncock made 262 career IndyCar starts and retired twice.

In 1967, joining A.J. Foyt as the sport's only owner/driver, and he was one of the last living drivers to have competed in both the front and rear-engine IndyCar eras. And like drivers from that generation, he also competed in NASCAR — making 21 starts, including three at the Daytona 500 where he finished fifth in 1973.

Johncock was inducted into the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Hall of Fame in 1997 and the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 1999.

Away from the track, Johncock loved farming and the forestry business — which explained his clothing choice and why people referred to his fashion choices as "Johncock casual."

He is survived by his wife, Sue; three daughters, two sons, two stepdaughters, 12 grandchildren, 17 great-grandchildren and one great-great grandchild.

They say the university's review of the Aug. 20 workout that left teammate Matthew Mayich on life support got key facts wrong and did not hold anyone responsible.

In their 26-page letter, sent through their attorney, Tim Casey, the players say Mayich never received water during a workout that ran more than 75 minutes. They also say he showed signs of distress long before he collapsed and was not properly cooled before paramedics arrived.

The ASU players sent the letter anonymously, writing that they fear retaliation from coach Greg Powers and his assistants, who "decide our playing time, scholarship levels, and roster status."

The news prompted Arizona's House and Senate education chairs to ask the Arizona Board of Regents Monday to retain an independent investigator to examine the incident.

The seven players who sent the letter make up roughly a quarter of the roster. They wrote that other teammates share their concerns but did not sign for the same reason. The letter says Casey holds "signed attestations" from the players confirming they are members of the team and were in attendance when Mayich suffered heatstroke.

"We should not have to choose between telling the truth about August 20 and keeping what we have worked our whole lives for," they wrote.

Along with leave for the staff who approved, ran and supervised the workout, the players also requested:

An investigation by "an agency outside the university"

Written assurance that no player will be punished for speaking out

An interim coaching staff during the investigation, naming former Coyotes captain Shane Doan as "an excellent candidate"

Mayich is a 21-year-old sophomore transfer from Stoney Creek, Ontario, in Canada. He had been in Arizona eight days when he collapsed at the end of the team's first preseason workout at Sun Angel Stadium. Family attorney Robert Carey has said Mayich suffered an exertional heatstroke that deprived his brain of oxygen and has no chance of a meaningful recovery.

2026-09-28 Hockey Team Members' Letter to ASU President Michael M. CrowDownload

The Sept. 28 letter responds point-by-point to the initial review by ASU Senior Vice President James Rund, delivered to Crow on Sept. 21.

The workout was run by Tim Ziesel, a former Green Beret whom an ASU booster introduced to the program.

ASU policy bars outside consultants from working with athletes until they are approved. Rund's report shows a request to use Ziesel was submitted Aug. 12 without a training plan, but the report does not say whether the request was ever reviewed or approved.

The players wrote that the only water break came 35 to 45 minutes in, not at 20 minutes as Rund's report found. When Powers told Ziesel to get the players water, Ziesel said, "Oh yeah, I forgot, you guys need water," according to the letter. Only the first eight or so players to finish a bear crawl reached the bottles, the letter said, adding that Mayich was still crawling and never received any water.

Rund's report said Mayich appeared to struggle during the final drill, a medicine-ball relay. The players wrote that he was disoriented much earlier and could not carry a teammate during a buddy-carry exercise. At one point, they wrote, he had to lean on a teammate to stay upright.

Ziesel left after assigning the medicine-ball relay, though Mayich was struggling before he left, according to the players. Only ASU coaches and an athletic trainer were supervising when Mayich collapsed.

"No one at ASU properly monitored him during the workout and no one intervened," the players wrote.

The players said the trainer sat Mayich upright twice, contradicting the report's statement that he was kept on the ground. The letter said Mayich lay in direct sun for several minutes. Cooling came from a few towels, squirt bottles and less than a minute of warm water from a garden hose, the letter said, despite ASU's heat policy calling for a cold-water immersion tub..

There was no tub on site, and no one used the tub inside Mullett Arena.

The players also dispute the report's statements that Mayich was acclimatized. They wrote that his only previous outdoor work was a few five-minute stretches broken up by breaks in air conditioning. They also cited a video of one drill showing the players in a "plank" position in direct sunlight, which contradicts the report's description of a mostly cloudy sky.

After an ambulance arrived and took Mayich to the hospital, the letter states, Powers told players he had "just a little heat stroke" and "just needs an IV." The next day, the players stated, the coach told them Mayich would be fine and the team went ahead with practice.

ASU opens its season at 5 p.m. Friday at Lindenwood. The letter asks Crow to act "if the facts in this report warrant it" and to name an interim coaching staff before the opener.

Meanwhile, House Education Committee Chairman Matt Gress, R-Phoenix, and Senate Education Committee Chairman Hildy Angius, R-Bullhead City, cite unresolved questions about whether ASU followed its own policies.

"Seven players who were on that field have raised serious questions that ASU's own review does not answer," Gress said in a statement. "We need an independent investigation to determine whether ASU followed its own rules, who was responsible for protecting these athletes, and what happened when Matthew Mayich showed signs of distress. ASU should not be left to investigate its own conduct and decide whether anyone should be held accountable."

title: How FIBA 3x3 Basketball Went From A Business Case To An Olympic Sport
description: FIBA 3x3 basketball evolved from a Youth Olympic experiment into a global sport, driven by gender equity, digital engagement and a spectator-first approach ahead of LA28.
fullText:
(This is part one of a two-part story based on a Forbes exclusive interview with Alex Sanchez on September 22, 2026. All quotes are taken directly from a transcript of the interview.)

In 2010, Alex Sanchez was not trying to save basketball, reinvent basketball or even necessarily build a new Olympic sport. He was doing something much more familiar to the world of business. He was analyzing an investment opportunity.

At the time, FIBA 3x3 basketball was being played at the Youth Olympic Games, but the International Basketball Federation wanted to know whether the abbreviated version of basketball was something more than a novelty. Could three-on-three basketball become a legitimate sport with its own athletes, competitions, commercial potential and global audience? Sanchez, who had an MBA from the University of Chicago and a background in private equity, venture capital and consulting, was asked to find out.

Sixteen years later, that analysis looks remarkably prescient.

Three-on-three basketball is now an Olympic sport, and it will arrive in Los Angeles for the 2028 Olympic Games with FIBA Managing Director Alex Sanchez still helping guide its global development.

"I did the analysis," Sanchez recalled in an interview with Forbes. "At the end of it … my conclusion at the time was that there was a real business case to develop 3x3 as a standalone discipline."

But there was an even bigger possibility. Sanchez concluded that 3x3 could become an Olympic sport if FIBA did the right things.

Sanchez's path to FIBA was not the conventional route for a basketball executive. Born in Barcelona to a Spanish father and German mother, Sanchez attended a German school in Spain and developed what he describes as two cultural perspectives on the same things. Before joining FIBA, he had already lived and worked in several European countries, including Spain, Belgium, Germany and the United Kingdom. He eventually came to the United States to earn an MBA at the University of Chicago, attracted in part by the finance-driven approach of the university's business program. After graduate school came private equity, venture capital and consulting.

The organization's previous secretary general wanted an objective analysis of 3x3. The sport was appearing at the Youth Olympic Games, but FIBA wanted to know whether there was a sustainable business proposition underneath it. Sanchez deliberately approached the assignment without treating it as a basketball project.

"I analyzed it as it would be a new brand for shoes or a new engine for planes," he said.

That distinction mattered. Instead of asking whether basketball fans liked three-on-three basketball, Sanchez was essentially asking whether a new sporting property could create a sufficiently differentiated product, audience and business model. The answer was yes. The next question was much harder: What would FIBA have to build to give 3x3 a legitimate opportunity to become Olympic? Sanchez and his colleagues produced a concept paper laying out what would have to happen.

That roadmap would require much more than changing the number of players on the court.

One of the first strategic decisions was gender equity. From the beginning, FIBA wanted men's and women's 3x3 to develop together. Sanchez said the organization was determined that national-team competitions would include men and women at the same time so the women's side would have an opportunity to grow at a comparable pace. The strategy was straightforward: If women's 3x3 were treated as an afterthought, it could fall behind.

Instead, gender equity became part of the architecture of the sport.

The second major milestone was professional competition. FIBA needed to demonstrate that 3x3 was not simply something athletes played occasionally at a Youth Olympic event. It needed professional athletes competing year-round. That led to the launch of the FIBA 3x3 World Tour in 2012, less than two years after FIBA's board decided to pursue the discipline. For Sanchez, this was critical.

"It had to have its own professional competition league tour," he explained.

The World Tour provided something that a collection of exhibition events could not: evidence that 3x3 could support a professional sporting ecosystem. It showed that athletes could make 3x3 their sport rather than treating it as a side activity.

And it gave FIBA an increasingly visible international product.

The next challenge was perhaps the most fundamental: What exactly should 3x3 basketball be?

FIBA could simply have taken traditional basketball, removed two players from each side and played the game on a half court. Instead, Sanchez said FIBA deliberately adapted the rules. The goal was to bring the organized version of the game closer to the way people actually played street basketball. That philosophy eventually became central to the sport's identity.

"The idea was to put the spectator in the center of all our changes or all our decisions," Sanchez said.

The objective was not simply to preserve basketball's traditional form. It was to create an experience. FIBA eventually described 3x3 with a simple phrase: "most thrilling urban sport." That phrase captured the strategy. The venues mattered. The rules mattered. The pace mattered. The presentation mattered.

And even the equipment became part of the product.

FIBA developed a ball specifically for 3x3. It is smaller than a traditional men's basketball but heavier, a combination Sanchez said was designed around the characteristics of the game and particularly outdoor grip and shooting. That might sound like a small detail.

The creation of a dedicated 3x3 ball was another indication that FIBA was no longer treating the discipline as simply a modified version of five-on-five basketball. It was becoming its own sporting product.

Perhaps the most interesting part of Sanchez's 3x3 strategy is that the sport was being designed for spectators before smartphones became the dominant way many younger fans consume sports. Today, that approach looks almost obvious.

A 3x3 game takes place on a half court with six players on the floor. The action is compact. The games are short. And the format naturally produces frequent highlights. Sanchez believes those characteristics make 3x3 particularly well suited for mobile viewing.

"You actually can see them everywhere," he said, referring to the short games and abundance of highlights.

That became an important part of FIBA's digital strategy. The organization created a social-media operation specifically focused on producing clips, polls and other digital content for platforms including Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and TikTok. The target audience was especially important. Sanchez said the core social audience falls largely within the 13-to-35 age range.

The sport therefore wasn't simply being played for the audience sitting courtside. It was also being packaged to be consumed by the person watching on a phone.

According to Sanchez, FIBA 3x3 now has more than 10 million social-media followers. Its dedicated social-media channels generate well above 1 billion views annually, according to Sanchez, approaching 2 billion views. Those figures are part of the story of how an experimental discipline became a global sporting property. But Sanchez believes another characteristic is just as important.

The audience is geographically distributed.

Rather than being concentrated primarily in one continent, Sanchez said 3x3 has developed meaningful participation and interest across Europe, the Americas and Asia. That distribution is rooted in something deceptively simple. A basketball hoop and a basketball are enough to begin.

As Sanchez put it, "if you have a ball and you have a hoop, actually, basically everybody will end up" trying to play.

That accessibility may be one of 3x3's greatest advantages.

For many basketball players, three-on-three is not something they learned from a federation. It is something they discovered after school at a park, in a driveway, or on an outdoor court with friends. The rules may vary. The competition may be informal. The stakes may be nothing more than bragging rights. But the fundamental experience is remarkably universal.

The beauty of the game was its simplicity. You didn't need a full roster, a coach or an elaborate facility. You needed a ball, a basket and somebody willing to play.

FIBA has taken that intuitive experience and built a professional sport around it without destroying the essence of the game.

title: US Senate passes landmark overhaul of college sports
description: The US Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.More than 30 million people watched January's college football national championship on TV while the major conferences -- regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights -- have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting con
fullText:
The US Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.

The bipartisan Protect College Sports Act would regulate how universities pay athletes, restrict transfers and give the governing NCAA limited protection from antitrust lawsuits after years of court battles transformed the economics of college athletics.

The vote was one of the Senate's last major legislative acts before lawmakers leave Washington to campaign for the November 3 midterm elections.

The bill now goes to the House of Representatives, which is already in recess until after Election Day, leaving a narrow window for Congress to complete work before a new legislature takes office in January.

President Donald Trump's administration has endorsed the legislation, and the 80-year-old leader himself cheered the bill's passage Monday night, posting to his Truth Social platform that "it will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves."

Unlike university sports in most countries, American college athletics is a vast commercial enterprise.

More than 30 million people watched January's college football national championship on TV while the major conferences -- regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights -- have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting contracts.

The legislation follows years of upheaval during which athletes won the right to profit from their names and images and, following a 2025 court settlement, universities began paying players directly.

It would establish national rules governing those payments and allow schools to spend nearly $50 million annually through revenue-sharing and other funds.

Athletes would generally be allowed one transfer without sitting out a season, while agents' fees would be capped at five percent.

The bill also provides longer-term scholarship and healthcare protections and seeks to safeguard women's and Olympic sports.

Supporters argue that nationwide rules are needed to replace a patchwork of state laws and repeated litigation.

"Student athletes deserve to get paid. They deserve real protections. And high school athletes deserve a fair shot to compete," said Senator Ted Cruz, who co-sponsored the bill.

"The Protect College Sports Act delivers that while protecting women's and Olympic sports and preserving the game we love for generations to come," the Texas Republican added.

But the measure has divided Democrats and drawn opposition from racial equality activists, labor unions and the Congressional Black Caucus.

Critics say its antitrust protections give too much power back to the NCAA while limiting athletes' legal rights and leaving unresolved whether college players should ultimately be treated as employees entitled to collective bargaining.

The House could seek changes, potentially forcing another Senate vote and complicating efforts to send the legislation to Trump before the current Congress expires.

title: Gordon Johncock, two-time Indy 500 winner, dies at 90
description: Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 winner and Motorsports Hall of Famer, died Monday, Sept. 28 at the age of 90, his family announced.
fullText:
Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 champion, died Monday, Sept. 28 in his South Branch, Michigan, home. He was 90 years old.

Johncock won the Indy 500 in 1973 and 1982. He is survived by his wife, Sue, five children – Peggy, Patsy, Pamilee, Wally and Gordon Jr. – stepdaughter (Valerie Heffelbowe), 12 grandchildren, 17 great grandchildren and one great great grandchild.

Johncock was not one to be in the light often. After his second retirement from racing, he owned Quigley Lumber, a Michigan business where he cut and sold timber.

"I've never been a person who wanted to be out in public and make appearances – I don't like that stuff," Johncock told IndyStar in 2016. "I've never said this before, but that's one reason I never pressured Roger Penske for a ride. He had his guys doing PR work constantly; there never was any relief.

"Although, if I had (joined Team Penske), I probably would have had a lot better record than I did."

Johncock was inducted into the IMS Museum Hall of Fame in 1997 and the Motorsports Hall of Fame of America in 2002. He won 25 races, 20 poles and the 1976 IndyCar (then USAC) championship. Johncock competed in 24 Indy 500s, finishing in the top five eight times and leading 339 laps. Johncock also started 21 races in the NASCAR Cup Series, although he was never a full-time driver.

Johncock said the 1982 Indy 500, which he won by just 0.160 seconds over Rick Mears, was the "biggest thrill" of his racing career. Johncock outdueled Mears, who has a record-tying four Indy 500 wins, by the sixth slimmest margin in Indy 500 history (at the time it was the closest margin). Johncock felt more gratitude for his second Indy 500 win after his first came in a rain-shortened, 133-lap race.

"The way it happened, the competition, so many near wins after 1973 and it all came together and the car lasted in 1982," Johncock said in 2023. "Plus I've got amazing respect for Rick Mears – one of the very best. He was never my teammate but I think we could have been good ones. I think the more pressure that was on me during a race the better I did and with the car pushing so bad and Rick on my tail, it was great. I'll never forget it. There are so many memories from that day – the crazy start, my final pit stop and winning by such a narrow margin – lastly pushing so hard the final laps with Rick in my mirrors."

Johncock was part of one of the most accomplished rookie classes in Indy 500 history in 1965. That was the same year that Mario Andretti and Al Unser debuted in the Greatest Spectacle in Racing. In Johncock's final Indy 500 start in 1992, he became the second oldest driver to compete in the race at 55 years and 272 days old. Only A.J. Foyt, who was 57 years and 129 days old in that same 1992 race, has done it at an older age than Johncock.

Johncock drove for most of his career at Patrick Racing, where he won both of his Indy 500s. He made 76 podiums in his career.

Zion Brown is IndyStar's motorsports reporter. Follow him at @z10nbr0wn. Get IndyStar's motor sports coverage sent directly to your inbox with our Motor Sports newsletter.

fullText:
Clippers news: LA sends strong message to fans at Media Day after Kawhi Leonard scandal appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

LOS ANGELES — The LA Clippers officially kicked off their season on Monday with Media Day at Intuit Dome. It was the first step in what will be a long journey back after the NBA handed down one of the harshest punishments in sports for their role in the Kawhi Leonard salary cap circumvention scandal.

In addition to the loss of five future first round draft picks, the NBA's punishment included a one year suspension for owner Steve Ballmer and a six month suspension for President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank.

That means general manager Trent Redden has been promoted to interim President and Mark Hughes is promoted to interim general manager.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Before Media Day officially kicked off with player interviews, Redden and Clippers head coach Tyronn Lue met with members of the media and provided a lengthy opening statement with regards to the NBA's investigation.

"Obviously, this took a little longer than we had hoped. You guys deserved to hear from us before this. Our fans deserved to hear from us before this. And for that, we're sorry. We've been listening, though, not just being quiet, but listening to the thoughts, the concerns, and feeling the emotions of our fan base. They mean everything to us. Their pain through this time is real. And we feel it and we hear them, as well as our staff members who are proud to be part of this organization. We hope to fulfill our promises to them to build their trust and move forward through this time.

"The penalties we are facing are significant and we will comply with it. It will go hand in hand with our mandate to our fans, to work to build their confidence as we go through the NBA's mandates and penalties this season. Personally, Ty and I are going to miss [Lawrence Frank] and Steve [Ballmer] immensely. We wouldn't be here if it weren't for them. And they have led us through a lot of different times. It will be a challenge without them, but what they prepared us for, although this unique circumstance is new. But the opportunities they've given us, the knowledge they've taught us will lead us, and they put together a staff that can offer us behind us and help fulfill all the things that we want to this season.

"In addition, Ty and I have both been able to meet with John Gibson, our interim governor, who is a leader and a steward for us during this difficult time, not just to us in basketball operations, but also on the business side. These challenges are large, not just the penalties, but some of the injuries that we've already faced as well. This franchise often has done its best work with his back against the wall. Training camp starts tomorrow. And we've got a deep group of players that have shown competitive spirit time and again, in a coaching staff led by Ty, who we thinks the best in the NBA. We hope to represent our fans the same way we always had in dark times by coming out and fighting."

Trent Redden opens up Clippers media day with a statement apologizing to fans and saying they’re listening to everything that’s been said about them. pic.twitter.com/QXc82eZdEN

— Tomer Azarly (@TomerAzarly) September 28, 2026

The statement is primarily directed towards the fans, who have been mostly neglected throughout this entire summer after the NBA came out and handed the Clippers their punishment for circumventing the salary cap with Kawhi Leonard.

Coach Tyronn Lue also added his statement on the morale of the LA Clippers franchise

"It's been difficult," Lue said. "Losing Steve and L. for this time, but I give our players a lot of credit. Since Day 1, we said we wanted everyone back the day after Labor Day, and we've had guys in the gym for two months now. Just working and trying to get better. I give our players a lot of credit for being here every single day. Everybody showed up. The leadership is great, the morale is great, even in these tough situations. That's good to see when you have your players coming in and giving everything that they have. A lot of teams don't have that."

The LA Clippers have traveled to Hawaii for training camp, where they'll be until they take on the Golden State Warriors on Sunday, October 4th.

title: Rams could be without starting cornerback, tight end vs. Eagles
description: Jaylen Watson and Terrance Ferguson are likely to miss Sunday’s game against the Eagles, while the Rams remain hopeful Puka Nacua can return
fullText:
The Rams' trip to Philadelphia is still several days away, but their injury concerns are already taking shape on both sides of the ball.

Los Angeles coach Sean McVay said Monday that cornerback Jaylen Watson dislocated his shoulder during Sunday's game against Denver and "probably" will miss Week 4 against the Eagles, according to Rams reporter Stu Jackson. McVay said the team has not discussed placing Watson on injured reserve. He has dealt with the injury before, ESPN's Sarah Barshop said.

Sean McVay said CB Jaylen Watson dislocated his shoulder. McVay said Watson "probably" will miss this week's game against Eagles, but he won't go on Injured Reserve. IR isn't something they've discussed.

Sean McVay said he imagines TE Terrance Ferguson will miss the Rams' Week 4 game against the Eagles with his ankle injury.

Terrance Ferguson also is likely to miss Sunday's game after suffering a medial ankle sprain. McVay described fellow tight end Colby Parkinson, who sustained an AC joint sprain in his shoulder, as more day-to-day. Those injuries could thin a group the Rams have used extensively in their passing game. Ferguson caught six passes for 54 yards and a touchdown against the Giants in Week 2. The Rams' participation reports later this week will better indicate who can play in Philadelphia.

The outlook is more encouraging for wide receiver Puka Nacua. McVay said he is "hopeful" Nacua will play against the Eagles after missing the Rams' past two games with a hip injury. Los Angeles had listed him as doubtful for Sunday's game in Denver. Watson's likely absence would affect the Rams' defense against Jalen Hurts and Philadelphia's receivers. Nacua's potential return could restore one of Matthew Stafford's top targets. Neither player has received a Week 4 game designation yet; those decisions will come after the teams practice this week.

EAST PROVIDENCE – Exactly how Providence Country Day or Bay View might match up against Cranston East will remain a mystery, but at least one question was answered Monday afternoon.

It will take a playoff meeting for anything to separate the Division III Knights and Bengals girls soccer squads. Injury Fund action couldn't do it, and this draw in the rain on the Providence Country Day campus also wasn't enough.

The elements would have been tricky enough to negotiate on the back end of this days-long storm. Add in a turf surface that played like lightning once it was wet and the conditions were too difficult for attackers to manage too many sharp chances. Providence Country Day keeper Iris Morkunas and Bay View keeper Taylor Pitney each kept a clean sheet while navigating a couple tense moments at each end.

The Knights (6-0-2) entered as winners of five straight and fresh off 36 goals in that span. The Bengals (5-1-1) held on at times but did enough to keep their city rivals away from goal. Giada Palano's sliding challenge late in the first half forced a deflected shot to loop over the crossbar and Pitney leaped just in time to stop a shot from distance in the second half that nearly bounced over her head and in.

Morkunas did her best work in the second half, particularly inside the final 10 minutes. Bay View earned a corner kick with the clock winding down and the ball was eventually played out to Kenzie Mooney about 30 yards from the left post. She cracked a right-footed drive that reached the cage on the fly, but Morkunas positioned herself perfectly to make a catch as the whistle sounded.

The two sides played to a 1-1 draw in late August and have since cruised through the regular season to date. The Bengals opened with a Division II loss against Burrillville but are unbeaten in six matches against their own table. Providence Country Day used a lone goal to beat Juanita Sanchez, 1-0, and was held to a scoreless draw by Davies before its recent sizzling streak.

The Thunderbolts entered the day a perfect 7-0-0 and don't have either Bay View or the Knights on their schedule during the regular season. They could avoid both sides all the way to the title match at Rhode Island College – this currently would be a meeting of No. 2 and No. 3 seeds in the bracket. Pawtucket, Johnston, Davies, Blackstone Valley Prep and West Warwick came into the week rounding out the top eight in the standings.

Eiley Simmons bagged the eventual winner and the Chargers added two goals just seconds apart to beat the Quakers, 3-0, in Division I.

Dylan Whitman set up the opener in the 53rd minute, dropping a pass for Simmons to force a deflected shot past the keeper. It stayed 1-0 until the 66th minute when Claire Short hit the top right corner to double the advantage. Maura Stelik put away a Morgan Brucker rebound just moments later as Chariho iced the result.

Savana Debont-Fitzgerald was forced to make just one save to earn the shutout, as the defense in front of her was strong from the Chargers (5-3-1). Marielle Nassiff made 10 saves for Moses Brown (1-5-0).

Maeve Soden continued her strong start to the season as the Avengers eased past the Falcons, 5-1, in Division I.

Soden triggered the attack with two goals and an assist, as East Greenwich built a 3-0 halftime cushion and never looked back. Claudia Hollingsworth, Maeve Monaghan and Izzy MacMillan each added a goal, Elizabeth Low dished out two assists and Vivien Marano chipped in another helper for the Avengers (5-2-0).

Abigail Frias netted a late goal in the second half for Cranston West (0-8-0). Alexa Ramirez finished with five saves.
